extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and researchers of U.S. history, propaganda, public relations, and wartime communications
extracted.subtask_description: Practices and standards used by a government wartime publicity body (the U.S. Committee on Public Information) for designing, producing, and coordinating mass persuasion across media and audiences. Covers messaging strategy, channels, training, audience targeting, and ethical/accuracy trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic multiple-reach messaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Creel set out to systematically reach every person in the United States multiple times with patriotic information about how the individual could contribute to the war effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate communications so target audiences encounter the same approved information repeatedly across channels to create unified public opinion; measure by frequency and penetration (e.g., number of exposures per person).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of short, volunteer public orations (Four-Minute Men)
rubrics_metrics.description: Four-Minute Men: 75,000 volunteers who gave short, patriotic speeches in public venues, such as movie theaters, to millions of Americans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design brief (≈4 minute) spoken messages for high-attendance interludes; recruit and train volunteers via local universities; provide pamphlets and speaking tips; encourage use of volunteers' own words while keeping messaging on approved topics (bonds, draft, rationing, recruitment, Red Cross).

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep messaging positive and avoid 'hymns of hate'
rubrics_metrics.description: Speakers were advised to keep their message positive, always use their own words and avoid 'hymns of hate.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize constructive, upbeat appeals (civic duties, contributions) rather than demonizing rhetoric; anti-pattern: mobilization based on hate (e.g., 'Stop the Hun!') can shift tone and cause ethical and social harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimedia, channel-diverse campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: The CPI used every medium available: posters, films, weekly newsreels, pamphlets, daily newspapers (Official Bulletin), news releases, radio, telegraph, slides (lantern pictures), and movies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ complementary channels (print, visual, film, live speech) to maximize reach; tailor content formats to each medium's affordances (e.g., striking imagery for posters, footage for newsreels).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor messaging to linguistic and ethnic audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Speeches were mostly in English, but ethnic groups were reached in their own languages. The CPI staged events designed for many different ethnic groups, in their language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Localize language and cultural framing; use community-specific events (e.g., concerts for Irish-American audiences) and materials to increase relevance and uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate with censorial/procedural partners to limit counter-propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: The committee worked with the Post Office to censor 'seditious' or anti-war materials, effectively controlling the flow of information; newspapers operated under 'voluntary' rules established by the CPI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish formal or informal cooperation with distribution/regulatory bodies to limit transmission of opposing messaging; note legal and ethical risks—such measures raise free-speech and civil-liberties concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use striking visual imagery and professional artists
rubrics_metrics.description: A Division of Pictorial Publicity created thousands of striking posters, including James Montgomery Flagg's iconic 'Uncle Sam Wants YOU,' and recruited prominent illustrators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission high-quality, memorable visuals and employ renowned artists/illustrators to increase salience and recall; produce a large volume of designs and materials for broad display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base messaging on facts but spin toward an upbeat narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: The CPI used material that was based on fact, but spun it to present an upbeat picture of the American war effort. Creel claimed the CPI routinely denied false or undocumented atrocity reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground content in factual claims while selecting and framing facts to support desired interpretations; the line between framing and deception must be managed—claims should be verifiable to maintain credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train communicators and provide topic-specific materials
rubrics_metrics.description: The speakers attended training sessions through local universities, and were given pamphlets and speaking tips on a wide variety of topics, such as buying Liberty Bonds, registering for the draft, rationing food, recruiting unskilled workers for munitions jobs, and supporting Red Cross programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide standardized training, talking points, and printed aids for messengers so they can confidently and consistently cover a set of policy topics and civic actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target messaging to specific demographic and occupational groups
rubrics_metrics.description: The committee also targeted the American worker and, endorsed by Samuel Gompers, filled factories and offices with posters designed to promote the critical role of American labor in the success of the war effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design campaigns and materials that speak to the interests, identities, and levers relevant to particular demographic or occupational segments (e.g., labor-focused posters in workplaces).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure consistency across channels and outlets
rubrics_metrics.description: Every item of war news they saw... was not merely officially approved information but precisely the same kind that millions of their fellow citizens were getting at the same moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate storylines, facts, and tone across newspapers, magazines, posters, and bulletins so audiences receive a unified message; use centralized editing/distribution (e.g., Official Bulletin) to enforce consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use historians and subject-matter experts to craft authoritative narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: Historians were assigned to write pamphlets and in-depth histories of the causes of the European war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage scholars and experts to produce longer-form explanatory content that lends legitimacy and context to campaign themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid premature or unverified public claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Media incidents: the CPI fed newspapers stories that were later discredited (e.g., claims of sinking submarines, fake plane photos); such exaggerations were challenged and mocked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify facts before wide dissemination; premature or fabricated announcements undermine credibility and can provoke public and press backlash—anti-patterns include embellished or fake images and unconfirmed battle claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor and adapt tone and portrayals in response to events
rubrics_metrics.description: As the war progressed, the depiction of the enemy evolved... by 1918 pamphlets depicted individuals of German descent living in the United States as a threat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust framing and target emphasis over time to reflect developments, but monitor ethical and social consequences of dehumanizing portrayals or targeting communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor overseas public diplomacy to local interests and media consumption
rubrics_metrics.description: The CPI extended its efforts overseas and found it had to tailor its work to its audience: in Peru there was an audience for photos of shipyards and steel mills; in Chile for public health and urban policing. It also provided reading rooms and language education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct audience analysis abroad and adapt content to local informational needs and cultural preferences; supplement media with services (reading rooms, education) to build goodwill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage celebrities, cultural figures and journalists for credibility and reach
rubrics_metrics.description: Famous illustrators and performers (e.g., John McCormack, Charles Dana Gibson) were brought together to produce and promote materials; American journalists with regional experience led Latin America efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use well-known artists, performers, and trusted journalists to lend credibility and increase audience attention and acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale distribution and measure reach
rubrics_metrics.description: The CPI distributed millions of pamphlets, produced thousands of poster designs and lantern slides, and Creel boasted of 7.5 million four-minute orations to over 300 million listeners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize mass production and distribution; track quantitative metrics (pamphlets printed, speeches delivered, estimated listeners/viewers) to assess campaign scale and penetration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance publicity claims with transparency about censorship and information control
rubrics_metrics.description: Creel wrote that the committee was 'in no degree... an agency of censorship' and emphasized openness, while in practice the CPI worked with the Post Office to limit anti-war materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of public claims about openness versus operational practices that restrict information; inconsistent messaging about transparency can invite criticism and investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid embellishing the truth to preserve long-term credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: One early incident demonstrated the dangers of embroidering the truth: the CPI fed newspapers a discredited story about escort ships sinking German submarines, which led to criticism and being called 'the Committee on Public Misinformation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain accuracy and avoid fabrications—short-term persuasive gains from falsehoods can lead to loss of trust and media skepticism.
